== Education ==

== Works ==
=== Drawings of real-life objects ===
Naderi Yeganeh has introduced two methods to draw real-life objects with mathematical formulas.<ref name="articlecosmos"/> By the first method, he creates tens of thousands of computer-generated mathematical figures to find a few interesting shapes accidentally. Then he changes the equations a little bit in order to increase the resemblance of the accidentally found shapes to real life objects.<ref>{{cite news |title=Math Is Beautiful |url=http://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/math-is-beautiful/ |date=19 January 2016 |first=Lauren |last=Young |work=[[Science Friday]] |access-date=23 January 2017 ==== ''A Bird in Flight'' ====
[[File:A Bird in Flight by Hamid Naderi Yeganeh.jpg|thumb|300x300px|A version of ''A Bird in Flight'' made up of 500 line segments, which Naderi Yeganeh created by his first method.]]
[[File:A Bird in Flight by Hamid Naderi Yeganeh 2016.jpg|300px|thumb|Another version of ''A Bird in Flight'' made up of 20,001 circles, which Naderi Yeganeh created by his second method.<ref name="American Mathematical Society">{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/publicoutreach/math-imagery/yeganeh|title=Mathematical Concepts Illustrated by Hamid Naderi Yeganeh|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|access-date=29 July 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190729162002/https://www.ams.org/publicoutreach/math-imagery/yeganeh|archive-date=29 July 2019|url-status=live}}</ref>]]
An instance of drawing real things by using Yeganeh's methods is ''A Bird in Flight,'' which is the name of a number of bird-like [[Geometric patterns|geometric shapes]] introduced by Naderi Yeganeh. Yeganeh created those drawings by using the two methods mentioned above. An example of ''A Bird in Flight'' that was created by his first method is made of 500 [[Line segments|segments]] defined in a [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian plane]] where for each <math>k=1, 2, 3, \ldots, 500</math> the endpoints of the <math>k</math>-th line segment are:

: <math>
\left(\frac{3}{2}\sin^7\left(\frac{2\pi k}{500}+\frac{\pi}{3}\right),\,\frac{1}{4}\cos^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi k}{500}\right)\right)
</math>

and

: <math>
\left(\frac{1}{5}\sin\left(\frac{6\pi k}{500}+\frac{\pi}{5}\right),\,\frac{-2}{3}\sin^2\left(\frac{2\pi k}{500}-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)
</math>.

The 500 line segments defined above together form a shape in the Cartesian plane that resembles a [[Bird flight|flying bird]]. Looking at the line segments on the wings of the bird causes an [[optical illusion]] and may trick the viewer into thinking that the line segments are [[curved lines]]. Therefore, the shape can also be considered as an [[Op art|optical artwork]].<ref name="American Mathematical Society" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name=":5">{{cite news|last=Mellow|first=Glendon|date=6 August 2015|title=Mathematically Precise Crosshatching|work=[[Scientific American]] (blog)|url=http://blogs.scientificamerican.com/symbiartic/mathematically-precise-crosshatching/|url-status=live|access-date=11 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925094554/http://blogs.scientificamerican.com/symbiartic/mathematically-precise-crosshatching/|archive-date=25 September 2015}}</ref><ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=เมื่อคณิตศาสตร์ถูกสร้างเป็นภาพศิลปะ|trans-title=When Mathematics is Made into Art|url=https://www.faa.chula.ac.th/SelfLearningFaamai/detailform/119|url-status=live|access-date=3 October 2021|website=Faculty of Fine and Applied Arts|publisher=[[Chulalongkorn University]]|language=th|archive-date=19 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210819233835/https://www.faa.chula.ac.th/SelfLearningFaamai/detailform/119}}</ref> Another version of ''A Bird in Flight'' that was designed by Naderi Yeganeh's second method is the union of all of the circles with center <math>\left(A(k), B(k)\right)</math> and radius <math>R(k)</math>, where <math>k=-10000, -9999, \ldots, 9999, 10000</math>, and
<div style=" line-height:6em;">
: <math>A(k)=\frac{3k}{20000}+\sin\left(\frac{\pi }{2}\left(\frac{k}{10000}\right)^7\right)\cos^6\left(\frac{41\pi k}{10000}\right)+\frac{1}{4}\cos^{16}\left(\frac{41\pi k}{10000}\right)\cos^{12}\left(\frac{\pi k}{20000}\right)\sin\left(\frac{6\pi k}{10000}\right), </math>
: <math>
\begin{align} B(k)= & -\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\left(\frac{k}{10000}\right)^7\right)\left(1+\frac{3}{2}\cos^6\left(\frac{\pi k}{20000}\right)\cos^6\left(\frac{3\pi k}{20000}\right)\right)\cos^6\left(\frac{41\pi k}{10000}\right) \\ & +\frac{1}{2}\cos^{10}\left(\frac{3\pi k}{100000}\right)\cos^{10}\left(\frac{9\pi k}{100000}\right)\cos^{10}\left(\frac{18\pi k}{100000}\right), \\ \end{align}
</math>
: <math>R(k)=\frac{1}{50}+\frac{1}{10}\sin^2\left(\frac{41\pi k}{10000}\right)\sin^2\left(\frac{9\pi k}{100000}\right)+\frac{1}{20}\cos^2\left(\frac{41\pi k}{10000}\right)\cos^{10}\left(\frac{\pi k}{20000}\right). </math>
</div>
The set of the 20,001 circles defined above form a subset of the Cartesian plane that resembles a flying bird. Although this version's equations are a lot more complicated than the version made of 500 segments, it has a far better resemblance to a real flying bird.<ref name="American Mathematical Society" /> It uses the periodic nature of trigonometric functions to form the feathers.<ref>American Mathematical Society (2026). Hamid Naderi Yeganeh: Mathematical Art. Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society. Available at: https://www.ams.org/publicoutreach/math-imagery/yeganeh. Accessed 4 Jan 2026.</ref>
Other works similar to this version of ''A Bird in Flight'' that was released by Naderi Yeganeh in 2016 are in the form of a flying [[parrot]], [[magpie]] and [[stork]].<ref name="huffblogbirds" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Gutiérrez Gómez |first=Margarita |url=https://letrame.com/catalogo/producto/artematicas/ |title=Artemáticas |publisher=Letrame Grupo Editorial |year=2023 |isbn=978-84-1144-491-0 |location=Spain |pages=135 |language=es}}</ref>

=== Fractals and tessellations ===
Naderi Yeganeh has designed some fractals and tessellations inspired by the [[continent]]s.<ref>{{cite news |title=The Tax Collector |url=http://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2015/04/13/finkel-4/ |date=13 April 2015 |first=Gary |last=Antonick |work=[[The New York Times]] (blog) |access-date=20 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150420002239/http://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2015/04/13/finkel-4/ |archive-date=20 April 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://mathmunch.org/2015/04/15/continents-math-explorers-club-and-i-use-math-for/ |title=Continents, Math Explorers' Club, and "I use math for…" |publisher=mathmunch.org |date=April 2015 |access-date=20 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150416073626/http://mathmunch.org/2015/04/15/continents-math-explorers-club-and-i-use-math-for/ |archive-date=16 April 2015 |url-status=live }}</ref> For example, in 2015, he described the fractal Africa with an [[Africa]]-like octagon and its lateral inversion.<ref name="articleguardian"/><ref name="London-Mathematical-Society-ref">{{cite web |url=http://education.lms.ac.uk/2016/08/hamid-naderi-yeganeh-fractal-africa/ |title=Hamid Naderi Yeganeh: Fractal Africa |publisher=The De Morgan Forum – [[London Mathematical Society]] |date=21 September 2016 |access-date=10 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161011055654/http://education.lms.ac.uk/2016/08/hamid-naderi-yeganeh-fractal-africa/ |archive-date=11 October 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="isfahanziba">{{cite news |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |date=20 October 2015 |title=با دنیای آدم های نابغه آشنا شویم، داوینچی ایرانی با فرمول ریاضی تابلو می کشد |trans-title=Learn about the world of geniuses, The Iranian da Vinci Draws Paintings by Mathematical Formulas |url=http://www.isfahanziba.ir/sites/default/files/newspaper/1394/07/28/pdf/15.pdf |language=fa |work=اصفهان زیبا |trans-work=The Beautiful Isfahan |location=[[Isfahan]] |access-date=23 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200223134609/http://www.isfahanziba.ir/sites/default/files/newspaper/1394/07/28/pdf/15.pdf |archive-date=23 February 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="imsnewsletter">{{cite news |date=Autumn 2015 |title=خلق آثار هنری به وسیله ی فرمول های ریاضی |trans-title=Creating Works of Art with Mathematical Formulas |url=https://ims.ir/files/publications/newsletter/ims_newsletter_145.pdf |language=fa |work=Newsletter of Iranian Mathematical Society |volume=36 |issue=3 |access-date=23 February 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170628032840/http://ims.ir/files/publications/newsletter/ims_newsletter_145.pdf |archive-date=28 June 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref> And he has created tessellations with [[Northern America]]-like and [[South America]]-like polygons.<ref name="articlseeker">{{cite news |last1=McDonald |first1=Glenn |title=Math Artist Finds the Beauty in Equations: Photos |url=https://www.seeker.com/math-artist-finds-the-beauty-in-equations-photos-1771197722.html |access-date=23 February 2020 |work=[[Seeker (media company)|Seeker]] |date=14 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200223202948/https://www.seeker.com/math-artist-finds-the-beauty-in-equations-photos-1771197722.html |archive-date=23 February 2020 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==== Fractal Africa ====
[[File:Fractal Africa 1 by Hamid Naderi Yeganeh.png|thumb|Fractal Africa]]

Fractal Africa is a [[fractal]] made of an infinite number of [[Africa]]-like [[octagon]]s which was introduced by Naderi Yeganeh.<ref name="articleguardian" /><ref>{{cite news|last1=Ouellette|first1=Jennifer|date=28 February 2015|title=Physics Week in Review: February 28, 2015|work=Scientific American|url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/cocktail-party-physics/physics-week-in-review-february-28-2015/|access-date=3 January 2021|archive-date=15 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200815000913/https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/cocktail-party-physics/physics-week-in-review-february-28-2015/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Paul |first=James |date=12 April 2024 |title=Mathematician Draws Sea Waves With Equations; Amused Internet Has Plenty Of Questions |url=https://in.mashable.com/tech/73151/mathematician-draws-sea-waves-with-equations-amused-internet-has-plenty-of-questions |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240412152025/https://in.mashable.com/tech/73151/mathematician-draws-sea-waves-with-equations-amused-internet-has-plenty-of-questions |archive-date=12 April 2024 |access-date=12 April 2024 |website=Mashable India |language=en-in}}</ref> The fractal's octagons are [[Similarity (geometry)|similar]] to each other and they have some resemblance to the map of Africa.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite web|author1=C.I.P. Citizens In Power|date=January 2020|title=TOOL 7: A SYNCHRONOUS EXHIBITION OF ARTMATH MASTERPIECES|url=https://artofmaths.eu/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/TOOL_7.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210102174738/https://artofmaths.eu/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/TOOL_7.pdf|archive-date=2 January 2021|access-date=21 March 2021|publisher=The Art Of Maths|page=9}}</ref> The numbers of octagons of different sizes in the fractal is related to the [[Fibonacci sequence]]: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, .... The height of the biggest octagon of the fractal is φ times larger than the height of second octagon; where φ is the [[golden ratio]].<ref name="London-Mathematical-Society-ref" /><ref name=":3" /><ref>{{cite news|last1=Antonick|first1=Gary|date=10 August 2015|title=John Conway's Wizard Puzzle|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2015/08/10/feiveson-1/|access-date=3 January 2021|archive-date=12 November 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201112024416/https://wordplay.blogs.nytimes.com/2015/08/10/feiveson-1/|url-status=live}}</ref><gallery widths="200" heights="200">
File:Fractal Africa and Fibonacci Sequence Animation by Hamid Naderi Yeganeh.gif|alt=
File:Fractal Africa and Fibonacci Sequence Animation 2 by Hamid Naderi Yeganeh.gif|alt=
</gallery>

successor?" for an article about him.<ref name="cnn article">{{cite news|date=17 September 2015|title=Math genius and artist: Is this the next da Vinci?|work=[[CNN]]|url=https://edition.cnn.com/videos/living/2015/09/17/math-art-style.cnn|url-status=live|access-date=2 March See more of...|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200310172820/https://twitter.com/MEIMaths/status/691946140745494528|archive-date=10 March 2020|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2016, Barbour Design Inc. stated on its own blog that "These often delicately intricate works are quite remarkable, and more astounding is that Yeganeh writes computer programs based on mathematical equations to produce them."<ref>{{cite web|date=5 April 2016|title=The Beauty of Math|url=https://barbourdesign.wordpress.com/2016/04/05/the-beauty-of-math/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200302161032/https://barbourdesign.wordpress.com/2016/04/05/the-beauty-of-math/|archive-date=2 March 2020|access-date=2 March 2020|publisher=Barbour Design Inc.}}</ref> In 2017, [[Mathematical Association of America]] commented about one of Naderi Yeganeh's animations in a tweet: "Watch the beauty of trigonometric functions come alive".<ref>{{cite tweet|user=maanow|author-link=Mathematical Association of America|number=868120851195023360|date=26 May 2017|title=Watch the beauty of trigonometric functions come alive}}</ref> In 2017, [[Fields Institute]] described Naderi Yeganeh's work as "beautiful math" in a tweet.<ref>{{cite tweet|user=FieldsInstitute|author-link=Fields Institute|number=923552360705732608|date=26 October 2017|title=Beautiful math...}}</ref> In 2017, [[Berkeley Lab]] commented on one of Naderi Yeganeh's blog posts: "Create stunning symmetrical images armed with a few equations and a computer".<ref>{{cite tweet|user=BerkeleyLab|author-link=Berkeley Lab|number=843939659394637824|date=21 March 2017|title=Create stunning symmetrical images armed with a few equations & a computer ...}}</ref>

== Views ==
Naderi Yeganeh believes that there are an infinite number of ways of using mathematical tools in art.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cook|first1=Katherine|url=|title=Art N Math|last2=Finkel|first2=Dan|date=13 March 2018|publisher=Center on Contemporary Art|isbn=9780999081921|location=|pages=|language=English}}</ref> In 2015, in an interview with [[CNN Style]] he said: "The power of mathematics is unlimited. There's an infinite number of great artworks that we can create".<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{cite web|date=26 September 2015|title=The Power of Mathematics is Unlimited!|url=https://www.mathnasium.com/http-cnn-it-1irqbna|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200320180536/https://www.mathnasium.com/http-cnn-it-1irqbna|archive-date=20 March 2020|website=[[Mathnasium]]|accessdate=20 March 2020}}</ref> He says, "I don't think computer-made art clashes with human creativity, but it can change the role of artists."<ref name=":0" /> In 2016, he said in an interview with [[Dong-A Science]]: "For me, mathematics is the best tool to create works of art."<ref>{{cite journal|author1=조혜인|date=July 2016|title=그래프의 화려한 변신|url=http://dl.dongascience.com/magazine/view/M201607N013|url-status=live|journal=수학동아 (Dong-A Mathematics)|language=Korean|publisher=[[The Dong-a Ilbo]]|volume=082|pages=62–65|issn=2092-6693|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200316082600/http://dl.dongascience.com/magazine/view/M201607N013|archive-date=16 March 2020|accessdate=16 March 2020}}</ref> Hamid Naderi Yeganeh believes that introducing mathematical objects that resemble real recognizable things may encourage young people to pursue mathematics.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Knowles|first1=Elizabeth|date=3 February 2016|title=When Math Transforms into Art|work=The Science Explorer|publisher=[[LabX Media Group]]|url=http://thescienceexplorer.com/technology/when-math-transforms-art|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191029121703/http://thescienceexplorer.com/technology/when-math-transforms-art|archive-date=29 October 2019|accessdate=12 March 2020}}</ref> He believes mathematics is an international culture and mathematics can help to promote peace and love between nations.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Pedersen|first1=Alex|title=CREATORS – HAMID NADERI YEGANEH|date=18 May 2016 |url=https://artthescience.com/blog/2016/05/18/creators-hamid-naderi-yeganeh/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200225133917/https://artthescience.com/blog/2016/05/18/creators-hamid-naderi-yeganeh/|archive-date=25 February 2020|publisher=Art the Science|accessdate=25 February 2020}}</ref> Naderi Yeganeh believes that [[Pi]] is an international number and it can be a [[symbol of peace]] between nations.<ref name="articlseeker" />
